beats.t: That morning, as the storeroom door opened, far upriver from the bakery, a black tiger crouched alone where the current broke white against the rocks.
Twelve marks from black hands remained on her back, wounds throbbing through her torn cloak. She didn't lick them. It felt like admitting pain.
Instead she felt inside her cloak. The wrapped bread was still there. Overnight, all its warmth had gone, leaving only its shape.
You said cold bread was just bread.
Beside it, a folded note held a name in crooked handwriting. The festival island's drummer child, whose applause the tiger had collected.
Are you still beating your drum? Even without applause?
The note didn't answer. She folded it again, her fingertips more careful than when closing a ledger.
She left the bread inside, only checking its place. The drummer's name, and the bread beside it. Now there were two things absent from the ledger.
She opened the ledger. No balance remained in Yeoni's column. Yet underneath, a faint new line spread, written by no one.
[ Ledger · Eulhae Yeoni · Uncollected: 1 ]
An outstanding debt?
A price uncollected, something still owed. She scratched at the line, but it grew clearer instead of vanishing.
What have I failed to collect? I took even that child's tomorrow.
As she spoke, a touch returned to her forehead: a child with nothing left pushing the ring with her own head, a voice saying to admit when it hurt.
The tiger had taken luck. Yet the ledger said she had received something herself. Something not yet repaid.
Then the black ring on her right forepaw glowed red. Each notch it tightened made a sound of crushed bone.
Ghh.
A black crack drew itself across the river, a gap pushed from another sky. A voice flowed through it along the ring.
Tiger. The paw that embraced my vessel is still attached, I see.
It is.
A pity. I should have taken it long ago.
The ring tightened again. Instead of screaming, she drove her claws into the rock and held on until the rock split.
Why didst thou come to me? Dost thou remember?
I came to stop that girl before she became a monster.
Aye. As she betrayed thee, one day she shall betray them all.
Who granted thee the chance to stop her?
You did.
Have you forgotten that kindness?
I have not forgotten. Not a single day.
And yet thou didst pull her from that river.
The tiger couldn't answer. Only the river sounded. Even she didn't know why she'd done it.
A scene rose instead of an answer. Not one she'd chosen. Whenever the ring tightened, this scene spilled out first.
A wet bench at a rainy bus stop. A hand tilting half an umbrella toward her. Rain always hid the face.
Then the same hand pushing her away. Whether it had truly been the same hand was always unclear.
The memory always broke there. Black Moon's voice filled the break. That girl betrays. That girl betrays.
One question. How much was that bread?
What?
A scent within thy cloak. One absent from the ledger.
Without thinking, the tiger wrapped her paws around her cloak. The gesture answered for her. Laughter came from beyond the gap.
Nothing is free. The price of that bread shall one day be claimed in blood.
I will pay for the bread. Please leave that bakery alone.
Oh? An order?
A request.
The ring gave one last hard squeeze. She toppled forward, face plunging into the river. Cold water flooded her nose.
I shall grant thy plea. Work for me in return.
The girl crossed to the human world this morning. That cat followed, wearing human guise.
Go thou also with a human face. The ending lies over there.
I lost my human face long ago.
I shall return it. A loan, of course. Thou knowest the interest.
Black fur flowed away like rain. Paws became hands, claws became nails, but the ring remained. It wound into the flesh of her right wrist as a thin golden band.
The gap closed. A wet-haired woman knelt beside the river, still holding the ledger.
After a long while, she searched her cloak. It was a black coat now. A note and a piece of bread lay in its inner pocket.
She unwrapped the bread. It was cold. She took a bite anyway.
Even cold, it held sweetness and butter. A flavor no ledger could record slowly spread over her tongue.
Her shoulders trembled once. She did not cry. Only rainwater ran down her face.
She ate half, then wrapped the rest and put it away. No one asked why. Even if someone had, she couldn't have answered.
On a rainy night, a fluorescent lamp flickered in an old apartment corridor. Of two neighboring doors at its end, one had a torn-cornered umbrella stand outside.
A black umbrella was propped before the vacant home next door. Water dripped from its tip onto the floor.
A door opened and closed. Only the smell of rain remained in the corridor.
Dust covered the empty apartment floor. Without turning on a light, the woman stood by the window. Water dripped from her coat.
Something fell beyond the thin wall. Then came a murmur like sleep talking.
Only one word came clearly through: socks. Rain covered the rest, hiding even whose voice it was.
She laid her palm against the wall. The gold band on her right wrist shone coldly. The murmuring stopped, as though someone sensed her even in sleep.
Noisy here too, I see.
She withdrew her hand, sat on the floor without removing her wet coat, and leaned against the wall until the sounds beyond it subsided.
In the ledger open on her knees, one outstanding debt glowed faintly in the dark. She watched the line a long time, then closed the book.
